video_title: Inside the AI Training Data Market — Gabe Greenberg, G2i
gist: G2I CEO Gabe Greenberg describes a bootstrapped human-data vendor growing from $15M to ~$100M revenue selling to five or six frontier labs, as demand shifts from mass labeling to staff-engineer-built RL environments priced by handling time. He argues labs buy fast and value quality over price, off-the-shelf non-exclusive data dominates, and the next frontiers are raw company data, robotics/3D, CAD and engineering domains.

insights.claim: G2I, a human-data and RL-environment vendor to frontier AI labs, did about $15M revenue last year, expects about $100M this year, is profitable with no VC backing, and says it could easily triple next year.
insights.speaker: Gabe Greenberg
insights.so_what: Bootstrapped ~6-7x growth signals extreme demand for post-training data; a likely private-market target or comp for Scale/Surge-style vendors.
insights.quote: last year we did 15 million. Uh this year will be about 100 million. No VC backing.

insights.claim: G2I's customer base is essentially five or six frontier labs, with second-tier labs buying data in proportion to the capital they raise.
insights.speaker: Gabe Greenberg
insights.so_what: Extreme customer concentration: vendor revenue tracks lab fundraising rounds, so lab capital raises are a leading indicator for data vendors.

insights.claim: G2I evolved from a React-focused engineering recruiting marketplace into a lab data vendor; the hiring marketplace is now very small and nearly all work goes to the labs, mirroring Handshake and about five similar marketplaces that pivoted at the same time.
insights.speaker: Gabe Greenberg
insights.so_what: Curated expert networks/recruiting marketplaces are a natural pivot path into AI data; look for similar pivots among talent platforms.

themes.theme: Shift from volume labeling to expert RL data

insights.claim: Human-data demand shifted from 2023-24 projects with ~6,000 modestly paid mid-level engineers doing gig-like work to smaller projects requiring staff-level engineers doing complex dataset building and 'taste' work, while robotics is restarting the high-volume collection cycle.
insights.speaker: Gabe Greenberg
insights.so_what: Value is migrating from low-cost labeling armies to high-skill expert networks; favors vendors with elite supply over crowd-work platforms.

insights.claim: RL training tasks must be calibrated to be just a few steps beyond current model capability: too hard and they become evals, too easy and they are worthless.
insights.speaker: Gabe Greenberg
insights.so_what: Task calibration is the core craft that differentiates premium data vendors; it also means data has a short shelf life as models improve.
insights.quote: if you make them too hard, they become eval, right? Uh and if you make them too easy, they're they're worthless.

insights.claim: Building RL environments involves anti-patterns relative to production software (verifiers, tasks, seed data), so even top engineers must be retrained; G2I screens by having candidates redesign a feature for an RL environment within 30 minutes.
insights.speaker: Gabe Greenberg
insights.so_what: RL-environment construction is a distinct, scarce skill set; training capacity is a moat for vendors.

insights.claim: SWE-bench, the top coding benchmark for over a year, began as an undergrad project with badly flawed instructions, and SWE-bench Pro also had major holes, illustrating that heavily adopted benchmarks need not be high quality.
insights.speaker: Host / Gabe Greenberg
insights.so_what: Be skeptical of benchmark-driven model rankings; benchmark quality is itself a business opportunity for data vendors.
insights.quote: anything that just gets a lot behind it, it doesn't need to necessarily be good

insights.claim: Benchmarks are getting harder, pushing labs from buying off-the-shelf data toward iterative partnerships where vendors refine everything from instructions down and bring research and gap analysis, not just people.
insights.speaker: Gabe Greenberg
insights.so_what: Partnership-style vendors with research capability should capture more wallet share and stickier revenue.

insights.claim: Frontier labs buy with no competitive RFP and very fast decisions; a researcher can spend $10M in 60 seconds, versus 6-12+ month procurement cycles at Fortune 50/100 enterprises, which Greenberg says is why enterprise 'AI transformation' is not actually happening.
insights.speaker: Gabe Greenberg
insights.so_what: Lab-facing vendors grow far faster than enterprise-facing AI vendors; enterprise sales cycles cap 'AI transformation' revenue near term.
insights.quote: a researcher in 60 seconds can spend $10 million

insights.claim: Labs now prioritize behavior and taste over raw correctness and benchmark volume, citing the refinement of Anthropic's Opus models as an example.
insights.speaker: Gabe Greenberg
insights.so_what: Demand is shifting to subjective, expert-judgment data that is harder to commoditize.

insights.claim: Quality now matters more than price: labs will not switch vendors for a 20% savings, and incumbents keep accounts until they screw up or are beaten on quality, like a trusted barber.
insights.speaker: Gabe Greenberg
insights.so_what: Data vendor relationships are sticky and price-insensitive, supporting durable margins for quality leaders.
insights.quote: quality data is now way more important than an a 20% price savings

insights.claim: Greenberg sizes the human-data market at a $10-15B+ total addressable market across coding, knowledge work and similar domains, with only two or three vendors above $1B revenue and everyone else below.
insights.speaker: Gabe Greenberg
insights.so_what: Concentrated but growing market; the sub-$1B tier is where consolidation or breakout candidates sit.

insights.claim: Labs avoid fully in-housing data work mainly due to complexity and legal/PR exposure of managing thousands of contractors (e.g. 6,000 people a month), not financial overhead; only one lab has a truly mature internal data operation (backed by a CEO blank check for data), and small in-house teams tend to get let go eventually.
insights.speaker: Gabe Greenberg
insights.so_what: Structural reason the outsourced data-vendor model persists even as lab spend grows.

insights.claim: Off-the-shelf data sold non-exclusively to multiple labs is the primary mode of business, and many labs accept it because it lowers their price; exclusivity mainly matters to the top one or two labs and niche datasets.
insights.speaker: Gabe Greenberg
insights.so_what: Data is less proprietary a moat than assumed; vendors can amortize dataset costs across labs, improving unit economics.
insights.quote: The competitive advantage only comes from the top one or two.

insights.claim: Data tasks are priced by average handling time (AHT); e.g. a long-horizon task might take a staff engineer paid $250/hour about 10 hours, with iterative rework loops on ~10% of deliveries.
insights.speaker: Gabe Greenberg
insights.so_what: Expert-hour pricing makes vendor revenue a labor-arbitrage business; watch expert wage rates as a margin driver.
insights.quote: AHT is kind of how you literally is how you price things

insights.claim: Security is a key failure mode for data vendors: a 500-person project means a 6,000-person funnel, with risks like North Korean infiltrators, supply-chain issues, leaked instructions, and contractors working for competing labs, yet vendors rarely lose status because few replacements exist.
insights.speaker: Gabe Greenberg
insights.so_what: Security posture is a diligence item for data vendors; limited vendor supply keeps switching low even after incidents.
insights.quote: how many people are from North Korea?

themes.theme: Data spend economics and demand outlook

insights.claim: The host argues post-training is now thick, sometimes consuming more compute than pre-training, and that data spend is moving from ~2-3% of compute budgets to ~4-6%, with a case for far higher since better data wastes less compute.
insights.speaker: Host (Latent Space)
insights.so_what: A 'scaling law of human data' implies data-vendor revenue grows faster than lab compute capex.

insights.claim: Labs ramp data purchases because idle compute is costly; they take 'good' data now over 'best' data later, and long-horizon data cannot be produced overnight unless off the shelf.
insights.speaker: Gabe Greenberg
insights.so_what: Compute build-outs pull forward data demand; off-the-shelf inventory has time value.
insights.quote: we're burning compute by letting it sit there

insights.claim: Greenberg frames data demand through Jevons paradox: unlike electricity, demand for intelligence is insatiable, so solving one benchmark always reveals longer-horizon, more specific and more expensive tasks.
insights.speaker: Gabe Greenberg
insights.so_what: Supports a secular rather than cyclical view of AI data spend.

insights.claim: Raw company data sales (e.g. a 50-year-old chemical engineering firm or a small beauty firm's Klaviyo/calendar data) are a 2026 theme, with G2I claiming 'ground zero' on raw data and million-dollar deals occurring; even a dying startup's Slack/email is sellable, but buyers now want at least a few terabytes and more than 10 headcount, up from 'anything' four months ago.
insights.speaker: Gabe Greenberg
insights.so_what: Corporate exhaust data is becoming a monetizable asset; potential new revenue line for data-rich legacy businesses.

insights.claim: Computer-use agents fail at entity resolution across tools (e.g. two similar names across Slack, email and HubSpot), so labs especially value cohesive data on the same project spanning GitHub, Linear and other tools.
insights.speaker: Gabe Greenberg
insights.so_what: Cross-application workflow datasets are the premium raw-data product for computer-use training.

insights.claim: Many lab researchers have startup ideas, so Greenberg expects many more neolabs and startups with verticalized harnesses around specific pain points.
insights.speaker: Gabe Greenberg
insights.so_what: Expect a wave of researcher-founded vertical AI startups, broadening the data vendor customer base beyond 5-6 labs.

insights.claim: The largest data vendors are betting on enterprises, which will need help buying data and building datasets, effectively creating 'neolabs inside every Fortune 500'.
insights.speaker: Gabe Greenberg
insights.so_what: Enterprise custom-model data work is the next TAM expansion for data vendors, though slowed by procurement.

insights.claim: Robotics, 3D world models, CAD and non-software engineering (mechanical engineering, chip design) are the next hot data areas, with legal, finance and computer use still having lots of room; robotics/3D buyers still sign six-month contracts whereas coding work no longer supports such horizons.
insights.speaker: Gabe Greenberg
insights.so_what: Earlier-stage data markets with longer contracts; watch vendors positioning in physical/engineering domains.
insights.quote: people will laugh at you if you talk about like 6 months

insights.claim: Greenberg expects more overt challenges to current model architecture next year and his holdco is evaluating an investment in a researcher aiming to cut inference cost ~50% with ~1% data loss.
insights.speaker: Gabe Greenberg
insights.so_what: Architecture challengers to inference cost could pressure inference-compute demand assumptions; uncertain if they work.
insights.quote: how can we cut inference by 50%. You know, and only have like a data loss of like 1%

insights.claim: G2I's Orc.ai is a Rust-built, self-hostable multi-agent orchestration platform with an SDK, used internally as a software factory and pitched to security, military/government and oil-and-gas customers as an opinionated framework for multi-agent governance and inter-agent comms.
insights.speaker: Gabe Greenberg
insights.so_what: Data vendors are productizing internal agent tooling into enterprise orchestration software, a possible second revenue engine.
